items.title: String theory is what happens when an intelligent system is starved of sensory input and starts hall...
items.content:
String theory is what happens when an intelligent system is starved of sensory input and starts hallucinating. Intelligence needs grounding.

For this reason, intelligence is practically never the bottleneck to solving impactful problems. The bottleneck is iterated contact with reality.

items.title:
Welcome to the era of embodied AI.

We are launching AA-Robotics v0.1, our research preview that mea...
items.content:
Welcome to the era of embodied AI.

We are launching AA-Robotics v0.1, our research preview that measures frontier language model performance on understanding, planning, and acting in the physical world. In v0.1, each model is given control of a 6-axis robot arm (5 joints and a gripper) and a simple objective. We’re releasing results for our first eight tasks today.

We find that frontier language models in coding agent harnesses have recently become capable of directly manipulating robot arms for simple tasks. Today, they are far too slow and expensive for any kind of production usage - nearly two orders of magnitude worse than human baselines. We expect this to change quickly.

GPT-6 Astra places first in AA-Robotics v0.1, followed by GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Opus 5.5.

AA-Robotics v0.1 details:

➤ Our first eight tasks test a range of capabilities: control and dexterity (precise grasping and object handling), spatial reasoning (how objects interact with one another) and adaptability (how models respond to the unexpected)

➤ Models get only brief instructions: how to connect to the robot arm (via a simple HTTP API), the arm's name and how to submit an attempt. They can view the scene through four cameras and write and run code to plan and send movements

➤ Once a model submits an attempt, its end state is graded against the task's pass criteria. A pass scores 100; an incomplete attempt earns partial credit. All attempts are zero-shot

Key findings:

➤ The GPT family tops the leaderboard: GPT-6 Astra scores 69, ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol at 65 and Gemini 4 Argon at 55. Claude Opus 5.5 (49) and Claude Fable 5.1 (46) trail

➤ Today’s models are incredibly slow at our tasks, taking ~30 minutes on average to complete each tabletop task

➤ Cost varies widely: GPT-6.1 Sol is the cheapest at $1.93 per task on average; GPT-6 Astra, the most expensive, costs $16.36, more than eight times as much

➤ Compared with a human, today's best-performing frontier language models are ~100x slower and ~10x more expensive

More results, clips, and how AA-Robotics v0.1 works follow in the thread below.

items.title: SpaceXAI’s Grok Voice 3.0 is the new leading Speech to Speech model, debuting at #1 on the Artificia...
items.content:
SpaceXAI’s Grok Voice 3.0 is the new leading Speech to Speech model, debuting at #1 on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Speech Index at 86.9, while also being competitive on latency

Grok Voice 3.0 is @spacexai 's successor to Grok Voice 2.0, a Speech to Speech model available through the SpaceXAI Realtime API at $0.08 per minute. We evaluated Grok Voice 3.0 with the Rex voice through the SpaceXAI Realtime API.

Key takeaways:

➤ Speech to Speech Index: Grok Voice 3.0 debuts at #1 at 86.9, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 83.2, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 82.6 and GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 80.1. It is up on Grok Voice 2.0 at 81.3 (+5.6 points) and Grok Voice 1.0 at 73.7 (+13.2 points), released just under six months ago. The Index averages Speech Reasoning (Big Bench Audio), Agentic Performance (Tau Voice), Arena Preference, and Task Success Rate

➤ Speech Agent Arena: Grok Voice 3.0 ranks #3 in preference at Elo 1070, behind Gemini 3.1 Flash Live Minimal (1100) and Gemini 3.8 Live (1088) and ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1057, and #1 on Task Success Rate at 94.8%, highest on the board, just ahead of Grok Voice 2.0 at 94.6%. Grok Voice 2.0 trails at Elo 1011

➤ Tau Voice: Grok Voice 3.0 takes the #2 spot on our Tau Voice benchmark implementation at 71.6%, behind GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5% and ahead of Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 68.6% and GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 59.3% - up from 56.5% for Grok Voice 2.0

➤ Big Bench Audio: Grok Voice 3.0 scores 98.5% on audio reasoning, ahead of Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 97.7% and Grok Voice 2.0 at 97.2%

➤ Speed: Average Time to First Audio on Big Bench Audio is 0.81 seconds for Grok Voice 3.0, well ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1.24s, GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 1.34s and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 1.35s, though slower than Grok Voice 2.0 at 0.70s

➤ Cost: Grok Voice 3.0 costs $4.80 per hour of input audio, the same as Grok Voice 2.0. That is above GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at $4.47 and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at $3.50, cheaper than GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at $5.83, and ~2.2x cheaper than GPT-Realtime-2.1 High at $10.75

Congrats to @elonmusk  and the @spacexai  team 🚀

See below for more detail ⬇️

items.title: We’ve added DeepSeek V4.1 Flash to AA-AgentPerf, with results for NVIDIA and AMD hardware. At 100 to...
items.content:
We’ve added DeepSeek V4.1 Flash to AA-AgentPerf, with results for NVIDIA and AMD hardware. At 100 tokens/s per user, NVIDIA GB300 is in first place with throughput up to 261M tokens/s per MW.

AA-AgentPerf is our agentic inference performance benchmark. It replays real agentic coding sessions, including prompt caching and tool-call delays, to give a realistic measure of inference performance in day-to-day agentic workloads. We measure total system throughput per megawatt of runtime power, and per-agent output speed at varying concurrency levels, to show the trade-off between system utilization and individual user experience.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash joins the leaderboard today. It brings the leaderboard to four featured models, joining DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.2/5.3. We are evolving the featured models as popular new open-weights models release, and will feature day-0 results for major future releases.

Background on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash:

➤ It scores 39 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, ahead of DeepSeek’s earlier V4 Pro 0813 at 36, with about a third of the parameters (552B ‘backbone’ and 16B active, against 1.6T and 49B)

➤ It is built on a new architecture, with a causal encoder-decoder design that activates 8B parameters per input token and 16B per output token. It uses a further 196B parameters of Engram n-gram memory that can sit in host memory rather than on the accelerator, and compressed sparse attention that needs about a quarter of even the earlier V4 Flash model’s KV cache per token

➤ This makes it much more efficient to serve, since the weights fit on fewer GPUs and the smaller KV cache leaves room for more concurrent agents per GPU

Initial AA-AgentPerf results for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash:

➤ V4.1 Flash runs on as few as 2 GPUs, so rack-scale systems get less advantage over 8-GPU single nodes like B300, which stays within about 20% of rack-scale GB300 NVL72 across the curve, and leads at both ends

➤ At 100 tok/s per user, GB300 leads with ~261M tokens/s per MW, ahead of B300 (~220M), B200 (~193M), GB200 (~178M) and MI355X (~128M)

➤ Every Blackwell system and MI355X can reach around 600 to 670 tok/s output speed for a single agent (ie. at batch size of one), against 372 to 392 tok/s on H100 and H200

➤ V4.1 Flash is both more intelligent than V4 Pro 0813 and much cheaper to serve, yielding ~1.3x (GB300) to ~6.2x (B200) the throughput per MW at 100 tok/s per user compared to its larger cousin

items.title: after switching our approach to building a "FirmOS", I'm increasingly confident that the future of a...
items.content:
after switching our approach to building a "FirmOS", I'm increasingly confident that the future of agent collaboration within organizational settings is going to be a "company operating system" or CompanyOS, designed for agent and human collaboration

instead of a "company brain" that holds everything, the OS is for storing rules, processes, decisions made, which tools to use and how. it can mirror some data, but the source of truth is often best held in your existing tools (CRM, etc.). it's continuously updated and used by your agents

i think of this as a "flipped playbook" where instead of writing down the company rules first and following them (which is kind of like waterfall development), you're constantly updating the playbook as you decide or learn new things day-to-day running the business

➤ Models run in an isolated container with brief instructions: how to re...
items.content:
How AA-Robotics v0.1 works

➤ Models run in an isolated container with brief instructions: how to reach the robot arm, which arm it is (a Hiwonder NexArm, with no further specifications), and how to submit an attempt as complete.

➤ They can view the scene through four cameras, three mounted around the table and one on the arm’s wrist, and can write and run code in the container to plan and send movements.

➤ Once a model has submitted a task for review, the end state is graded against the task’s pass criteria. A pass scores 100, with points awarded for partial success in the case of an incomplete task. All task attempts are zero-shot.

items.title:
Yes, I have so much time now

I honestly feel like we're entering a new time of leisure where people...
items.content:
Yes, I have so much time now

I honestly feel like we're entering a new time of leisure where people are just talking to their agents to steer the direction of our work, while they work in the background 24/7

Like @felixrieseberg did while building his new homepage literally on a bike ride while talking to Claude on iOS

I already kinda did this with scheduled cron jobs for years, my sites were almost fully automated, but I still had to add features or fix bugs sometimes, but now for a year or more that part is also fully automated by AI

So then we just have so much leisure time suddenly available, that we can spend time with the ppl we love, do more fun things, play games, work on our health/fitness, be outside more, etc. 

Some of that freed up time now goes into new projects, but there's a certain level of creative expression for me where it's sufficient and I am starting more and more to see I am spending that way from a computer screen too, and prefer it that way

Maybe this is the new time where we can finally live not work, as it was predicted 96 years ago by Keynes. That prediction never really came to fruition though because the automation that was invented just moved the work up to higher level (like from making actual things to financial, managerial, administrative, etc.) and people chose to just consume more, so they had to work more again!

But maybe now is different though, it definitely feels different to me

items.title: Cambrian Capital's @_Lonis_ explains why a $150 silicon wafer that turns into $22,000 worth of chips...
items.content:
Cambrian Capital's @_Lonis_ explains why a $150 silicon wafer that turns into $22,000 worth of chips could be one of the biggest overlooked investment opportunities in AI:

"We’re somewhat less interested in energy because there’s so much latent energy and so much latent tooling you can pull in."

"The problem with the semi supply chain, the silicon, is that there’s no latent supply. Everything is almost in short supply. You have all these bidders for these very scarce inputs."

"We like to go really far up in the supply chain, so go to suppliers of the suppliers. It’s less priced in there and fewer people are looking. Silicon wafers is one example. A small oligopoly of makers that are making these $150 hyper-thin, hyper-smooth silicon wafers that make up the chips."

"They have the least price elastic customer base of any part of the supply chain, because they make a $150 product that turns into $22,000 worth of chip. So they can almost arbitrarily double, triple prices in theory, and it wouldn’t really matter to the end margin of the chip maker."

He notes a $150 wafer becomes $22,000 worth of chips, wafer makers form a small oligopoly with scarce, inelastic supply, and unlike energy there is no latent tooling or supply to expand quickly, giving suppliers outsized pricing power.

Anyone can build an agent that fills out forms and clicks buttons, but that won't make a good booking agent.

items.content:
Evals?!?!?!

As you all know, I dislike public benchmarks, but we do have to measure intelligence somehow.

We are trying an experiment in communicating our internal measure of intelligence.

See the blog for more details, but don’t treat it like it’s absolutely gospel, and you don’t even have to believe it fully, and it’s likely biased to our models so feel free to only pay attention to the relative ranking of open models. Shout outs to the Kev guy!

(We did not include hosted models because of what they do with their data and we want to keep our validation set very secure…)

items.title: This is exactly what I see everywhere I go and what I hear from everyone I talk to: they need more p...
items.content:
This is exactly what I see everywhere I go and what I hear from everyone I talk to: they need more people, not fewer.

In fact, many companies are telling me they are stuck because they can't find enough talent in the market.

They are already using the latest-and-greatest AI-thingies out there, but they don't have enough warm bodies to operate them.

These agents aren't magic. They, for the most part, aren't autonomous. They are cool and all, but they need people who know their stuff.

This is even more acute for building software. Yes, anyone can vibe-code simple apps here and there today, but building working software for thousands of user is still very demanding, and agentic coding helps but doesn't work without experts driving it.

items.title: Asana CPO @ArBose explains why AI has made writing code the easy part of software development, while...
items.content:
Asana CPO @ArBose explains why AI has made writing code the easy part of software development, while deciding what to build has become the real bottleneck:

"Because the cost of writing code has dropped so dramatically with coding agents, what’s become way more important is getting aligned on the strategy, on the outcomes you’re trying to build, and ensuring your entire R&D team are aligned on those outcomes."

"Even two years ago, the most interesting cost was ensuring that the developer was spending the right time on the right ticket."

"Now it’s figuring out what tickets do you even want to prioritize, and are they written with the right level of context so that the coding agent gets it right the first time, versus get back some slop that you’ll end up rewriting."

"You go from high quality PRDs that generate agent-ready tickets, and you can trigger these swarms of coding agents in whatever coding agent of choice. We partner with OpenAI Codex, we partner with SpaceXSI’s Cursor, we also have integrations with GitHub Copilot live right now."
@asana

items.title: MI355X has its strongest showing on DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813. It serves ~15% to 40% more throughput per ...
items.content: MI355X has its strongest showing on DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813. It serves ~15% to 40% more throughput per MW than B200 between 35 and 75 tok/s per user, peaking at about 94M tokens/s per MW at 33 tok/s per user, a level B200 only reaches at 13 tok/s. Above about 80 tok/s per user B200 pulls ahead, and for a single agent the gap becomes MI355X at 240 tok/s vs. B200 at 367 tok/s. Disaggregated multi-node configs for other NVIDIA hardware largely sit above both, e.g. with B300 at 125M tokens/s per MW at 116 tok/s per user using two 8-GPU nodes.

items.title: LLMs can answer questions about graphs, but it remains unclear whether training makes them reason re...
items.content:
LLMs can answer questions about graphs, but it remains unclear whether training makes them reason reliably when graphs grow or change. This matters for applications that combine graph data with text, where converting graph structure into a long textual prompt can become inefficient or unreliable. The article systematically compares training strategies and tests not only familiar tasks, but also larger graphs, unfamiliar graph structures, and related tasks the models were not trained to perform.

The article evaluates six approaches using synthetic directed graphs: supervised fine-tuning, prompt tuning, two variants of reinforcement learning, and graph-encoder tokens used either alone or alongside graph text. Its main experiments train on four basic tasks—counting nodes, finding a node’s degree, and two forms of reachability—using graphs of 5–20 nodes. The evaluation includes graphs up to 160 nodes, new structures such as trees and long cycles, and four related tasks withheld from training. Answer distributions were controlled so that performance could be compared against a clear chance baseline. The study focuses mainly on a 4-billion-parameter model, with additional tests on larger and differently designed models.

Read with an AI tutor: https://t.co/nhniBQKkaN

items.title: As AI agents increasingly access business data through repeated cycles of reasoning and database que...
items.content:
As AI agents increasingly access business data through repeated cycles of reasoning and database queries, the amount of schema information sent to a language model can become a major cost and performance bottleneck. Large catalogs consume tokens, add processing delay, and may distract the model with irrelevant tables and columns. Yet schema-retrieval systems are commonly judged by recall alone—whether they include all information needed for a query—which can make sending an entire catalog look ideal despite its high cost. The article argues that this mismatch can lead organizations to choose systems that are expensive and less effective in practice.

The article proposes evaluating schema retrieval with three complementary measures: useful schema coverage per token, total token use across a multi-step task, and estimated cost per reasoning step. To show how these measures can inform system design, it also builds a prototype that first retrieves likely relevant tables, then scores them more closely, and preserves necessary links between tables so the resulting schema remains usable for joins. The prototype was tested on 1,000 queries from the BIRD-SQL benchmark, using schemas substantially smaller than the thousands-of-table catalogs that motivate the work.

items.content:
Cambrian Capital's @_Lonis_ reveals why a researcher at a major AI lab is stockpiling Unitree robots from China, betting that AI will soon solve the missing piece of robotics:

"I just met recently with a robotics person at one of the big labs. His thesis was that most of robotics is actually solved in terms of the body. What’s not solved is the brain."

"So he’s stacking up all of these Unitree robots from China, hoping that the brain is solved soon, and then the value of this physical input goes up a lot."

"While China is struggling massively to catch up in the chip supply chain, because there’s all of these decade-old industries in South Korea, Taiwan, Japan that they have to build up from scratch, we’ll have the same problem in the West when it comes to robotics. We don’t have any of those supply chains."

"It’s not even trivial for us to figure out how to invest in it, because we can’t arbitrarily invest in Chinese markets for regulatory reasons."

items.content:
Cambrian Capital's @_Lonis_ reveals why Wall Street is still missing the next AI revolution, which he believes could be far bigger than coding agents:

"They have smart people. They’re great at finance stuff. But they’re not really seeing the different paradigms of use cases."

"Most people here in the Bay were vibe coding in March or April. The rest of the world didn’t start vibe coding until January and February of this year."

"Same thing now, where people in the Bay are starting to vibe work, as I call it, using computer use. The people on the street don’t have that intuition about this new use case, which in my opinion will be way larger than coding agents even. There’s just way more white-collar workers."

"Memory is trading at five times earnings. We might be able to double production by end of decade on memory bits. Maybe 2.5x at most. Then you go to Wall Street and they say, ‘We think we’ll have oversupply again.’ It’s very hard to square oversupply, when we only can 2.5x by end of decade, with the short timelines."

items.title: LLM serving must balance response speed, processing capacity, and energy use. One proposed approach ...
items.content:
LLM serving must balance response speed, processing capacity, and energy use. One proposed approach assigns separate GPUs to the two stages of inference: processing the input and generating output tokens. This separation can reduce interference between stages and allow them to be tuned independently, but it also requires moving a large intermediate data store—the key–value cache—between GPUs. The article tests whether disaggregating the stages delivers practical benefits once the transfer method and energy costs are considered.

The article benchmarks disaggregated serving against a two-GPU setup in which each GPU handles both stages for half the requests. It compares cache transfer over a high-speed GPU link, over PCIe, and via disk. Using two language models, synthetic workloads with different batch sizes, and one server equipped with two NVIDIA A100 GPUs, the authors measure latency, throughput, and energy. They also vary GPU operating frequencies to test whether independently tuning the input-processing and token-generation stages can improve efficiency while meeting latency targets.

items.title: Cambrian Capital's @_Lonis_ explains why he's extremely bearish on software stocks, as AI labs devel...
items.content:
Cambrian Capital's @_Lonis_ explains why he's extremely bearish on software stocks, as AI labs develop internal models far more powerful than anything they release publicly:

"We’re super bearish. We’re hyper bearish. If you remove the memory companies, most of the enterprise value in AI currently is just software companies. Chip designers and networking designers. It’s just the first thing the labs will compete with."

"There will be this larger and larger chasm between the quality of the models they’re able to release externally and the ones they have internally. They will just have way better models internally that they’ll use to design better chips. It’s very hard to compete with that for any software company."

"These software companies are trading at way higher multiples than the physical parts companies. Going forward, we really don’t see that making sense. If you have physical inputs and you need to reinvest, at least you’re worth the higher multiples because you have some type of moat."

items.title: Vector symbolic architectures (VSAs) encode symbols and structured information in high-dimensional v...
items.content:
Vector symbolic architectures (VSAs) encode symbols and structured information in high-dimensional vectors, enabling compact, parallel operations that may suit energy-efficient computing. Their practical use depends on a basic design question: how large must the vectors be to support reliable tasks such as checking whether a symbol is present or estimating how much two sets overlap? The article addresses this question with formal capacity bounds, replacing much of the earlier reliance on empirical performance with guarantees about accuracy and failure probability.

The article analyzes four VSA designs—two based on dense signed vectors and two based on sparse binary vectors—and introduces a modified associative-memory network called Hopfield±. Using mathematical analysis of randomly generated representations, it derives bounds for membership checks and set-intersection estimates, as well as for selected operations involving sequences and bound key–value pairs. A central approach connects vector representations to data-sketching methods, including Johnson–Lindenstrauss projections, and to Bloom filters. The authors also handle dependencies among vector entries that arise in some operations, rather than assuming all components behave independently.

items.title: Robinhood VP @abhishekf96 explains why people will trust AI agents to text their friends long before...
items.content:
Robinhood VP @abhishekf96 explains why people will trust AI agents to text their friends long before they trust them to manage their money:

"Finance is so personal for people. You’re gonna be much more likely to have your agent text a friend for you than manage your finances for you. So I think the trust journey on finance is gonna be a little bit longer than other everyday tasks."

"Robinhood in 2013 was one of the first mobile-only investing apps. People downloaded it a lot, but it was kind of a side account. They’d put $500 into Robinhood and say, ‘Let me just try this out.’ And then over the course of a decade, Robinhood has become the primary place to store wealth for so many people."

"We’ll probably go through a similar journey with Robinhood Agents, where people will trust it with a side part of their money that they wanna experiment with, and then over time it’ll grow. I don’t think that cycle will be 10 years."
@RobinhoodApp

items.title:
Expanding:

Lightcone Commons accepts a range of grant proposals.  Recommenders rank them by priorit...
items.content:
Expanding:

Lightcone Commons accepts a range of grant proposals.  Recommenders rank them by priority order.  Funders direct money to recommenders (and potentially veto particular items) (or can fund items directly).  Then "the obvious" algorithm reconciles all the priorities, to avert the usual problem in charity where everybody delays hoping that somebody else will fund something.

The total amount of money Lightcone Commons has to dispense, is much less than the amount of grant proposals that Nate Soares thinks could be usefully funded.  He thinks he can direct an additional $50M, or $90M, or $150M.  (With noticeable downticks in the utility of the last marginal dollar after each interval.)

My guess is that my own unfunded priority ranking has a further $10M of good room that wouldn't overlap with Nate's.  (This doesn't reflect deep disagreement, probably, but that we went through different fractions of an enormous flood of grant proposals.)

While we're on the subject, Lightcone Infrastructure recuses themselves from being an LC funding recipient because they are just that scrupulous.  LI is NOT adequately funded.  I would put the first $5M to Lightcone Infrastructure above literally anything else on my priority list, if you're taking recommendations from me.  And then the next $10M to Lightcone ahead of anything after the first 20 grants on my list.

So if you're trying to figure out how to usefully increase the scale of your giving by $70M within the next month or so, talk to myself or Nate, please?

Even if you're merely trying to scale up your giving another $10M, you could join Lightcone Commons as a funder on the current round and direct it to Nate.  (Or myself, or split with some of the other recommenders, &c.)

It is nicer and makes better incentives for everyone if the added funding happens in time to be reconciled into the collective priority order calculated on Oct 23.  But I suppose LC would figure out how to direct a sufficiently large chunk of money if it came in Oct 24 instead.  (There's another planned funding round for December, if this one goes well, but who knows what the AI landscape will look like by then?)

Blatant lies to the contrary, our supposedly vast anti-extinction conspiracy remains much less funded than the AI industry.  But we are trying hard to scale up to be more the counterforce they allege we are.

items.title: MI355X has its strongest showing on DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813. It serves ~15% to 40% more throughput per ...
items.content: MI355X has its strongest showing on DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813. It serves ~15% to 40% more throughput per MW than B200 between 35 and 75 tok/s per user, peaking at about 94M tokens/s per MW at 33 tok/s per user, a level B200 only reaches at 13 tok/s. Above about 80 tok/s per user B200 pulls ahead, and for a single agent the gap becomes MI355X at 240 tok/s vs. B200 at 367 tok/s. Disaggregated multi-node configs for other NVIDIA hardware largely sit above both, e.g. with B300 at 125M tokens/s per MW at 116 tok/s per user using two 8-GPU nodes.

items.title: The most popular textbook on multiagent systems and algorithmic game theory (aka the MAS book), than...
items.content:
The most popular textbook on multiagent systems and algorithmic game theory (aka the MAS book), thanks to the permission given by its generous authors, is now on @ChapterPal. The textbook is used at thousands of universities around the world, and now you can read it with an AI tutor.

Multiagent Systems: Algorithmic, Game-Theoretic, and Logical Foundations by @yshoham and @k_leyton_brown provides an advanced, mathematically formal presentation of systems populated by multiple autonomous entities with diverging information or conflicting objectives.

Intended for researchers and graduate students across computer science, operations research, and related mathematical fields, it presumes comfort with formal mathematical reasoning, basic algorithms and computational complexity, elementary probability theory, linear and integer programming, classical logic, and basic Markov decision processes.

The central focus is the computational dimension of multiagent interactions, combining principles from artificial intelligence, economics, and mathematical logic into a cohesive theoretical framework.

Read the MAS book on ChapterPal with an AI tutor: https://t.co/reh70OmWEJ

Table of contents:

Introduction

Distributed Constraint Satisfaction

Distributed Optimization

Introduction to Noncooperative Game Theory: Games in Normal Form

Computing Solution Concepts of Normal-Form Games

Games with Sequential Actions: Reasoning and Computing with the Extensive Form

Richer Representations: Beyond the Normal and Extensive Forms

Learning and Teaching

Communication

Aggregating Preferences: Social Choice

Protocols for Strategic Agents: Mechanism Design

Protocols for Multiagent Resource Allocation: Auctions

Teams of Selfish Agents: An Introduction to Coalitional Game Theory

Logics of Knowledge and Belief

Beyond Belief: Probability, Dynamics and Intention

Appendices: Technical Background

items.title: Asana CPO @ArBose argues that today's AI chat interface is fundamentally broken, predicting a future...
items.content:
Asana CPO @ArBose argues that today's AI chat interface is fundamentally broken, predicting a future where AI agents know what you need before you even ask:

"I don’t think that many enterprises actually have long horizon agents running today. Almost everybody is using the chat tools to create content or to summarize meetings. In a year’s time, it’ll be the norm for long horizon complex workflows to be agentic."

"I think the current user experience for engaging with AI is broken. It’s a chat window. You have to come up with the creativity to ask it questions or provide it with a blurb of text and context and hope that the result is good."

"Proactivity is gonna be the big sea change, and it’ll take the impact of AI from a small percentage of people who actually use it today on a day-to-day basis to the mainstream."
@asana

items.title: The PDF to Markdown converter that is used internally on ChapterPal to ingest scientific papers and ...
items.content:
The PDF to Markdown converter that is used internally on ChapterPal to ingest scientific papers and books is now available as a standalone tool: https://t.co/3bN7sDWPoK

The Premium OCR returns high-quality validated markdown files, one per chapter, as well as the images of all illustrations.

All math is converted into LaTeX. Tables are converted into their \begin{tabular}...\end{tabular} equivalent unless they contain graphics. In this latter case they are extracted as images.

Algorithms are extracted as images. Code blocks are extracted as ```language...``` blocks.

All captions are semantically linked to their objects.

Give it a try and let me know if anything didn't work out as expected.

items.title: Tempo CBO @dwr predicts AI agents will soon have their own financial accounts, allowing them to nego...
items.content:
Tempo CBO @dwr predicts AI agents will soon have their own financial accounts, allowing them to negotiate bills, collect refunds, and manage money on your behalf:

"In terms of the actual numbers of agentic transactions, those are still small. That’s across the board, not just stablecoins."

"In the last 6 to 8 weeks, we’ve seen a lot of excitement around personal agents. Instinct, Meta’s Muse product, ChatGPT just released Dots. 6 months from now, virtually every consumer platform with some level of scale in AI is going to have some type of personal agent product, and those personal agents are going to be doing transactions for people."

"There is a real opportunity for agents with wallets, because agents are not creatures of habit like humans, so they’re able to simultaneously use both cards and stablecoins."

"There’s a lot of focus on how can I spend money, but there’s a version of the world where, how can I actually receive money? Receiving a refund, or negotiating your bill down and those funds coming back to a stablecoin wallet that your agent is managing. A lot of these personal agents with wallets are gonna start to resemble proto-financial accounts."
@tempo

A st...
items.content:
When a sandbox resumes on another machine, it keeps its sandbox ID but starts a new execution.

A stale route can send a valid request to the older execution and return old data. Checking the sandbox ID alone won’t catch the difference.
items.author: @perplexity_ai

items.content_html:
When a sandbox resumes on another machine, it keeps its sandbox ID but starts a new execution.

A stale route can send a valid request to the older execution and return old data. Checking the sandbox ID alone won’t catch the difference.

items.title: In addition to our new DeepSeek V4.1 Flash results, we’re adding AMD’s MI355X to AA-AgentPerf for Ki...
items.content:
In addition to our new DeepSeek V4.1 Flash results, we’re adding AMD’s MI355X to AA-AgentPerf for Kimi K3, GLM-5.2/5.3 and DeepSeek V4 Pro - comparing it to our latest results for NVIDIA systems on coding agent workloads.

AA-AgentPerf is our agentic inference performance benchmark. It replays real agentic coding sessions, including prompt caching and tool-call delays, to give a realistic measure of inference performance in day-to-day agentic workloads.

MI355X is AMD's flagship accelerator in the MI350 series, launched in June 2025 on its CDNA 4 architecture. It has the same 288GB of HBM3E at 8TB/s as NVIDIA's B300, around 10 PFLOPS of dense FP4 compute (vs. B300 at ~13.5 and B200 at ~9) and board power of up to 1,400W. All our MI355X results use ROCm nightly and dev builds of vLLM and SGLang.

We are debuting results for AMD's MI355X on a single 8-GPU node across all four featured AA-AgentPerf models. Results on our leaderboard are live and will evolve over time - we look forward to tracking software/serving improvements on AMD hardware.

Initial results on MI355X:

➤ Its strongest result is on DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813, where MI355X serves ~15% to 40% more throughput per MW than B200 between 35 and 75 tok/s per user, likely helped by its 288GB of HBM per GPU (B200 has 180GB) on a 1.6T parameter model

➤ On DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, MI355X is in line with NVIDIA Blackwell for a single agent at 647 tok/s (B300 at 652, B200 at 669), but falls behind as load rises, reaching ~128M tokens/s per MW at 100 tok/s per user against ~193M for B200 and ~220M for B300

➤ On GLM-5.2/5.3, MI355X trails B200 and B300 at 100 tok/s per user, with ~26M tokens/s per MW against ~42M and ~44M respectively

➤ On Kimi K3 (2.8T parameters), MI355X serves ~8M tokens/s per MW at 50 tok/s per user against ~24M for B300 using NVIDIA's multi-node configs, and 152 tok/s for a single agent against 235

items.title: Tempo CBO @dwr warns that AI is destroying the illusion of privacy in crypto, making it easier than ...
items.content:
Tempo CBO @dwr warns that AI is destroying the illusion of privacy in crypto, making it easier than ever for competitors to track transactions on public blockchains:

"When you send a stablecoin payment on a blockchain, that’s public. People have this false sense of, no one knows what I’m doing on a blockchain. We now have AI. It’s really much more straightforward for a determined adversary or competitor to map out everything that’s happening on-chain."

"If you’re a business using stablecoins, all of your other payment methods that you use with customers are private, and then when you’re using stablecoins, they’re public."

"We built Zones to bring the privacy that enterprises expect to Tempo. Whether you’re using them publicly or privately, that just becomes a flip of the switch."
@tempo

items.title: The Hundred-Page Machine Learning Book by Andriy Burkov is widely considered an excellent, high-qual...
items.content:
The Hundred-Page Machine Learning Book by Andriy Burkov is widely considered an excellent, high-quality book, but its usefulness depends heavily on your background.

It has earned semi-cult status and high praise from industry leaders at Google, Amazon, and LinkedIn for doing the "impossibly hard task" of condensing an immense field into roughly 140 pages. However, because of this extreme compression, it functions more like a dense, mathematically rigorous map than an easy-to-read beginner's guide.

What Makes It Good:

- Incredible Breadth and Efficiency: It manages to pack supervised learning, unsupervised learning, neural networks, ensemble methods, and feature engineering into a book you can read in a week.

- High-Level Overview without Fluff: It strips away the historical filler found in 800-page textbooks and focuses strictly on "what works" in the industry.

- Strong Reference Material: Experienced engineers and graduate students praise it as a highly reliable, compact refresher for math formulas and machine learning architecture.

The author offers a "read-first, buy-later" policy, and you can browse a free PDF on the book's official website (https://t.co/alpqEeQ2vz) to see if the math level suits you before buying a physical copy.

items.content:
Tempo CBO @dwr explains why trillions of dollars in stablecoin transactions are a misleading measure of adoption, and why crypto's real revolution is only just beginning:

"The expansion of financial services with stablecoins is the trend to watch."

"A lot of data with stablecoins tends to focus on these very large numbers, hundreds of billions, trillions of dollars moved on blockchains. There’s a lot of noise in that data. You have a lot of trading that’s happening on chain, but it’s maybe not the most economically productive activity. The real world use cases of stablecoins are just starting."

"I’ve been in crypto for a decade. This is actually where crypto is starting to impact regular people’s lives. Can I actually spend it? Can I get my money paid out faster? Can I earn a bit of upside?"

"Those are the core things that are gonna scale the impact of crypto that we’ve all been waiting for."
@tempo

items.title: Last year, I met the guy who owns this $30 million 1959 Jaguar, which was the first car to have disc...
items.content:
Last year, I met the guy who owns this $30 million 1959 Jaguar, which was the first car to have disc brakes and won a lot of races back then. I asked the owner, "Why do you collect cars like this?" He said, "I want to have a time machine, one that takes me back to the past."

Well, tomorrow we're going to see Tesla introduce a car that instead takes you to the future: or "back to the future," as Christopher Lloyd's character in Back to the Future showed us, which is why I'm sharing this item.

When @elonmusk gave me a ride in the first Roadster as I was blessed to have the first ride, even before he gave a ride to his best friend. He broke three laws, three traffic laws, in demonstrating Tesla's first product. 

I wonder how many laws he's going to break tomorrow demonstrating this new Roadster. I imagine it'll break a few.

For instance, up to now, car designers have always wanted to keep their tires in contact with the pavement. If you lose contact with the pavement, you lose control. It'll be real interesting to see what it does when it loses contact with the pavement. :-)

I'm jealous of anybody who gets a ride in this one, but I wouldn't trade my first ride with anybody who's getting a ride tomorrow. I'll get a chance soon enough.
